card.title: The unit circle behind every identity

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: On a circle of radius 1 the point at angle θ has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ), so the horizontal leg is cos θ and the vertical leg is sin θ — every trigonometric identity is that one right triangle rearranged.

figure.caption: Unit circle: radius 1, cos θ as the horizontal leg and sin θ as the vertical leg.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: x = cos θ, y = sin θ;  x² + y² = 1;  sin²θ + cos²θ = 1;  tan θ = sin θ / cos θ

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: θ is measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis and must be in radians in calculus; wherever cos θ = 0 the tangent is undefined.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: 30°, 45° and 60° give the standard ratios, and the maximum of a sin θ + b cos θ is √(a² + b²) — the amplitude circle's radius.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: The circle fixes the sign by quadrant but says nothing about triangles beyond 180°, which is where the CAST rule and the general solution take over.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Right triangle with hypotenuse 1 ⇒ x = cos θ, y = sin θ;  Pythagoras gives x² + y² = 1 ⇒ sin²θ + cos²θ = 1

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Learn the circle instead of four quadrant rules: read the sign of cos θ off the x-axis and the sign of sin θ off the y-axis.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Using the unit circle, prove sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 and find every θ in [0, 2π] for which sin θ = 1/√2.
